text: Why don't billionaires ever leave their money directly to their children?
Meet Rick. One billion dollars. One son.
If Rick just leaves it to him when he dies, the IRS shows up first.
The estate tax: forty percent on everything above fifteen million.
That's almost four hundred million dollars. Gone.
So rich families play a different game. They don't own. Their trusts do.
Years earlier, Rick moves his company shares into an irrevocable trust.
Back then, they were worth fifteen million. That fits his tax-free limit.
Then the company explodes. Fifteen million turns into one billion. Inside the trust.
That growth was never Rick's. So the estate tax never touches it.
His son doesn't own a dime. He's just the beneficiary.
The trust buys the mansion, the cars, the jet, and lets him use them.
Sued? With a spendthrift clause, his creditors usually can't reach it.
Divorce? Trust money usually stays out of the split.
And some of these trusts can last for generations.
The rich don't own more on paper. They own less.
